articleTitle: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
summary: Amazon announced the Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam, autonomous security devices that use cameras, on-device sensors and cloud processing to map indoor spaces and navigate patrol routes. The article details their operating limits and privacy concerns, including the drone’s pending FCC authorization, Ring’s prior FTC investigation and the EFF’s criticism of Ring’s encryption.

2K video resolution.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: Amazon promotes the new Ring Robotics products as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” citing recording indicators and notifications. Amazon says their videos will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption, introduced in September 2026.
coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The EFF describes Throw Away the Key Encryption as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings but still well short of end-to-end encryption. It also criticizes Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach and Ring’s reintroduction of features allowing law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access. Ryan Calo previously warned that flying security cameras create new ways to surveil others indoors and give companies greater access to sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: A 2023 FTC investigation charged Ring with allowing employees and contractors to watch recordings of customers’ private spaces; the FTC also described safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts. The Ring Always Home Cam, temporarily available by invitation as a Day 1 Edition product in September 2021, previously prompted privacy concerns. Amazon says the Rover was inspired by customer feedback about the invite-only Amazon Astro home-monitoring beta. Separately, the Familiar Faces facial-recognition feature available for fixed Ring doorbell cameras starting in December 2025 is the subject of a class action lawsuit.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: Both devices’ AI Pilot systems use cloud processing, not solely on-device processing.
Both devices digitally map the customer’s home or business floor plan.
Drone setup requires the customer to carry it through indoor spaces; Rover setup involves autonomous exploration.
The Ring Drone Cam still requires Federal Communications Commission authorization before sale; January 27, 2027 is Amazon’s conditional target.
The drone’s set-route and scheduled-patrol capability requires an Amazon Ring Protect subscription.
The drone’s stated 8 minutes of flight time applies to a new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions.
Drone navigation may degrade around polished marble or wet tile, featureless blank matte walls, frameless glass and mirrors.
The Rover is limited to a single-floor, indoor environment and cannot climb stairs.
The Rover is incompatible with curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.
Rover videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events are stored in the cloud for up to 180 days.
The EFF says Throw Away the Key Encryption remains well short of end-to-end encryption.

The article reports no current mention of facial recognition or similar person-identification technology in the new Ring Robotics products; the Familiar Faces feature and associated class action lawsuit concern fixed Ring doorbell cameras.
